string.text: The .45 ACP cartridge with a full metal jacket bullet has remained popular for more than a century. Its heavy projectile, propelled by a relatively mild powder charge, travels at modest velocity but delivers substantial stopping power.

A non-standard variant of the .45 ACP cartridge, featuring a semi-jacketed hollow-point bullet with a steel core. This combination of expanding and armor-piercing characteristics inherits both the strengths and weaknesses of each type.

The 5.7x28 SS190 cartridge was originally developed in the mid-1980s for the FN P90 submachine gun. Later, the Five-seveN pistol was designed as a companion weapon for the same cartridge. The round offers strong stopping power and can penetrate most body armor.
A standard 12-gauge shell loaded with 6 mm buckshot. At close range it delivers tremendous lethality and stopping power. Intended exclusively for use in smoothbore firearms.

A 12-gauge shell loaded with an unjacketed solid projectile. Commonly used for hunting large game but suitable for other purposes as well: its heavy slug does not pierce armor so much as punch through it by sheer force.
The 5.45x39 mm 7N22 armor-piercing cartridge is used in assault rifles of multiple Warsaw Pact states. Inside the bullet is a hardened alloy penetrator core. Highly effective against body armor.

The 5.45x39 mm 7N10 cartridge, featuring a bullet with enhanced penetration, is used in assault rifles of many Warsaw Pact countries. Reduced recoil impulse and increased bullet flight range provide higher accuracy compared to the older 7.62 mm round.
A NATO cartridge with enhanced armor-piercing capability, known as SS109/M855. Effective against body armor and widely used in military and law-enforcement firearms throughout the West.
A low-impulse NATO cartridge designed for accurate burst fire. Known under the designation SS109. Offers excellent ballistic performance.

A Soviet pistol cartridge that earned its reputation during World War II and maintained popularity during the crime waves of the 1990s. Due to the vast stockpiles remaining in military depots, it is inexpensive and widely circulated in the Zone. Offers decent penetration, though its stopping power is inferior to that of modern alternatives.
A sniper-grade 7.62 mm cartridge featuring a steel-core projectile. Compared to the standard round of the same caliber, it offers superior ballistics and improved penetration.
An inexpensive standard 7.62 mm cartridge. Due to its design, it is unsuitable for precision sniper fire and is typically used in automatic weapons where extreme accuracy is not required.
Beneath the bullet’s metal jacket lie a steel penetrator and a lead shell. Provides good stopping power but is ineffective against body armor.

A high-impulse cartridge developed specifically for the PMM pistol. Compared to the standard 9x18 mm round, bullet velocity is significantly increased due to a 15% rise in chamber pressure. However, this also accelerates barrel wear. Ineffective against body armor.
A standard 9x19 mm cartridge with a full metal jacket bullet. Noted for good ballistics and low production cost, which led to its widespread adoption. Poor performance against body armor.
A semi-jacketed hollow-point bullet offering high stopping power and low ricochet risk. Commonly used as a "police" or civilian self-defense round. Ineffective against body armor.

The subsonic SP-6 "automatic" cartridge uses a semi-jacketed bullet with a partially exposed hardened-steel penetrator core. Requires a suppressor for effective covert use. Widely used in several Warsaw Pact countries. Effective against body armor.

The subsonic SP-5 sniper cartridge features a bi-metal jacketed bullet. The cavity behind the steel penetrator is filled with lead. Requires a suppressor for covert firing. Distributed among special-purpose units of various Warsaw Pact states.

The .50 Action Express is the most powerful pistol cartridge in the world. Weapons chambered for it are rare among stalkers, making the ammunition itself uncommon in the Zone. Primarily used for hunting large or exceptionally large game.

A pistol cartridge with enhanced armor-piercing capability. Intended for defeating personnel protected by individual armor. The hardened steel penetrator protrudes from the jacket, giving the bullet exceptional penetrating performance.
High-technology power cells for the Gauss rifle, manufactured under controlled industrial conditions using advanced equipment.
These lower-capacity cells use capsulated fragments of the Flash artifact as their power source. Their lower capacity is due to makeshift production conditions and lack of specialized equipment.
A 40 mm grenade for underbarrel launchers. Compatible with most NATO service weapons. The effective fragmentation radius is approximately 5 meters.
An improved 40 mm grenade used in NATO launchers. Designed specifically for engaging targets behind cover.

The PG-7VL round is intended for RPG-7-series launchers. Its rocket motor allows it to strike concealed enemies at considerable distances. Its relatively poor accuracy is offset by the large blast radius.
A Soviet caseless fragmentation grenade used primarily with the GP-25 "Koster" launcher. The effective fragmentation radius is about 5 meters.
An improved caseless underbarrel grenade used in Soviet and Russian weapons, offering better effectiveness against concealed targets.
